Chronology of Russian History

Introduction

I know of no other nation whose history offers as much 
depth, intrigue and richness as the long, complicated history of Russia. Though the Cold 
War raised the level of consciousness of Russians amongst Westerners, it arguably did so 
in a skewed fashion. The mass media that regularly broadcast the Cold War ensured that 
nearly everyone had some familiarity with the likes of Lenin, Stalin, and Brezhnev, but 
regrettably little mention was made beyond scholarly circles of the previous 1,000 years 
of abundant, fascinating Russian history.

My goal here is to provide the general reader with 
stimulating articles on all recorded years of Russian history, beginning from Kievan Rus' 
to Yeltsin's era in the 1990s. Though I will use scholarly-accepted resources, there is 
always room for lively debate on the information, as many decisive elements in Russian 
history have been contested by recognized scholars for centuries. 

Because Russia never formed part of the Western Empire, nor 
was it ever civilized from Rome, the traditional divisions of historic studies (ancient, 
medieval, modern) do not fit here. The history of Russia is more fittingly divided whereby 
the periods correspond to the epochs in which various cities were the capital of the 
Russian state -- Kiev, Moscow, St. Petersburg, and Moscow again. From the time that the 
first state originated about the end of the ninth century around Kiev, Russian history has 
essentially been the tale of these three cities: Each served as a capital of a sprawling 
Slavic empire on the eastern periphery of Europe, and each had an indelible impact on 
modern Russian culture. In the words of a Russian proverb, Moscow was the heart of Russia; 
St. Petersburg, its head; Kiev, its mother. 

History:
 
pre-revolutionary 
russia and the Soviet union

In the course of the 9th century, Viking 
tribes from Scandinavia moved southward into European Russia, tracing a path along the 
main waterway connecting the Baltic and Black Seas. The first monarchic dynasty, which 
ruled until the Mongol invasion of the 13th century, built Kiev as its capital. The Mongol 
Empire, which stretched across the Asian continent, was divided into a number of 
â
hordes
â
 or 
individual kingdoms; Russia was put under the suzerainty of the Khanate of the Golden 
Horde. The next two centuries saw the rise of Moscow as a provincial capital and centre of 
the Christian Orthodox Church. In the late 15th century the Grand Prince of Moscow, Ivan 
III (the Great), annexed the rival principalities of Russia, including the Novgorod 
Republic to the north, thus becoming the first national sovereign. His grandson Ivan IV 
(better known as Ivan the Terrible) further expanded the state to the south and into 
Siberia. He was the first to hold the title of Tsar (derived from 
â
Caesar
â
). The 
political history of the period from 1500 until the mid-17th century was characterised by 
struggles between the tsar and the rich, powerful landed nobility, known as the 
boyars
. 
The Russian empire expanded gradually to acquire land to the south as far as the Caspian 
Sea and eastwards into Siberia. The two most important rulers of Russia in the 17th and 
18th centuries were Peter the Great (1682-1725), who cemented the regime and established 
Russia as a leading European power, and Catherine the Great (1762-96), generally 
recognised as an astute and energetic ruler, who pursued a policy of enlightened despotism 
at home while continuing the aggressive foreign policy initiated by Peter. In the first 
quarter of the 19th century, under Tsar Alexander I, the first steps were taken to 
dismantle the system of serfdom under which most people lived. The process was disrupted, 
however, by Napoleon
â
s invasion of Russia. The French were driven out in 1812 and 
Napoleon
â
s army destroyed in the legendary retreat from Moscow. Alexander
â
s successor 
completed the growth of the empire into the Caucasus (now Georgia) and Armenia and reached 
agreement with England about the division of Central Asia into spheres of influence. Most 
of Siberia had been annexed by the 1840s, but the expansion to the south and east 
(creating more or less the present frontiers of the CIS) was not complete until 1905. 
Domestic policies remained conservative: pressure for political and economic reform was 
met only with repression. By February 1917, the populace engulfed Russia in widespread 
strikes, rioting and army mutinies, which forced the Tsar to abdicate. The liberal 
Provisional Government which took control was forced out of office by a Bolshevik coup in 
October of that year. The Bolsheviks (majority faction) were the more radical product of 
the split in the Social Democratic Party, formed in 1898, upon which much of the organised 
opposition to the regime was focused. Under the leadership of Vladimir Ilich Ulyanov, 
better known as Lenin, the Bolsheviks moved quickly to consolidate their position, 
bringing land, industry and finance under state control. Within two years, having seen off 
the military challenge of the right-wing White Armies backed by the major European powers, 
who sought the re-establishment of the tsarist regime, the Bolsheviks were firmly in 
control. Lenin died in 1924 and was succeeded by Josef Stalin (Djugashvili) who instituted 
a crash programme of industrialisation and the forced collectivisation of agriculture. 
Famine and massive purges were the hallmark of this period. In 1941, the USSR was invaded 
by Nazi Germany, despite having signed a peace treaty with Hitler in 1939, in the start of 
what Soviets referred to as the Great Patriotic War. Like Napoleon before him, Hitler
â
s armies 
were driven out, again with massive loss of life on the Russian side (an estimated 20 
million people). A large reconstruction effort had, by the early 1950s, repaired much of 
the war damage. In the meantime, the USSR had become the world
â
s second nuclear power, 
having exploded its first atomic bomb in 1949, and sponsored the formation of a buffer 
zone of communist-controlled governments in Eastern Europe. The occasional instability of 
these regimes led the USSR to intervene militarily on two occasions 
â
 in Hungary 
in 1956 and in Czechoslovakia in 1968. Foreign policy has since been dominated by 
relations with the USA, which fluctuated from outright hostility to the 
â
Cold Peace
â
 of 
dÃ©tente. The two sides came to the brink of nuclear war in the 1962 Cuban missile crisis. 
The Soviet Union was by now in the hands of Stalin
â
s successor, Nikita Krushchev, who shocked the 
Communist Party in 1956 by revealing the extent of Stalin
â
s brutality. Also during 
Krushchev
â
s term, the split with China, which fractured the unity of the world 
communist movement, took place; the two countries have been at loggerheads ever since. 
After Krushchev
â
s fall from power in 1964, the USSR was led until 1982 by Leonid 
Brezhnev. In retrospect, the Brezhnev years are seen as a period of stability and 
relaxation in international tensions (although he took the USSR into Afghanistan) coupled 
with domestic stagnation and inertia, presided over by an ageing and unimaginative party 
leadership. The very last General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, 
Mikhail Sergeyevich Gorbachev, took over the leadership in March 1985, after a 3-year 
inter-regnum of two General Secretaries, Andropov and Chernenko, who were more often than 
not indisposed by ill health. Gorbachev instigated a programme of social, political and 
economic reform, and a wholesale diplomatic offensive abroad, not only on nuclear arms 
control, but also in regional policies and relations with the Third World. An early 
success for Gorbachev was the treaty on Intermediate Nuclear Forces, signed in December 
1987, which eliminated a whole category of superpower nuclear armaments. Another 
protracted dispute with the Americans was settled in early 1989, when the last Soviet 
forces left Afghanistan after a decade of fighting. At home, Gorbachev
â
s programme 
centred on the slogan-concepts of 
perestroika
 (restructuring) and 
glasnost
 
(openness). At the heart of the 
glasnost 
policy was the liberalisation of the 
media, which have since played an important role in bringing to popular attention policy 
errors and official mismanagement, previously hidden from most people. When Gorbachev took 
office he declared that the 
â
nationalities problem
â
 
â
 a 
reference to 100-plus distinct ethnic groups in the Soviet Union 
â
 was the 
most serious facing the nation. He was quickly proved right as the relaxation of the state 
stranglehold over the country
â
s political and social life allowed simmering 
aspirations and resentments to come to the surface, particularly in the southern republics 
of Trans-Caucasia and Central Asia. As the dire state of the economy became apparent, the 
Soviet Union all but ceased to be a player on the international arena, illustrated by its 
lack of reaction to the Kuwait crisis of 1990 (where the Soviet Union meekly followed the 
US line) and its lack of resistance to Western terms on the reunification of Germany. 
Gorbachev made his final stand by setting himself firmly against the dissolution of the 
USSR, despite growing demand in the republics for independence. The Baltic Republics were 
particularly adamant on this issue and organised plebiscites which proved that 
independence enjoyed overwhelming popular support. Gorbachev
â
s disastrous decision to 
send the Red Army into Lithuania in early 1991 to prevent it from seceding, marked the 
beginning of the end. Squeezed by radicals and secessionists on one side and conservative 
elements in the military and KGB on the other, Gorbachev
â
s position was becoming 
increasingly untenable. At this point a rival emerged 
â
 sacked head of the Moscow 
Communist Party, Boris Yeltsin, who won the election for the presidency of the Russian 
Republic in June 1991. This conferred on Yeltsin a legitimacy which Gorbachev, who had 
never received any popular mandate, could not match. Meanwhile, the conservatives in the 
party, the army and the KGB looked on with increasing horror realising that if they were 
going to arrest the transformation of the country (and with it their own positions), they 
would need to act quickly. On August 19, 1991, while Gorbachev was holidaying in the 
Crimea, a coup was staged by the 
â
State Committee for the State of Emergency in the 
USSR
â
. Badly planned, it fizzled out after three days, but Gorbachev
â
s position 
had been completely undermined. Boris Yeltsin, who co-ordinated and rallied resistance to 
the coup, came out greatly strengthened. Gorbachev
â
s last attempt to save the USSR was dismissed by the 
leaders of the republics who spent the remaining months of 1991 consolidating their own 
positions and sketching the rough outline of a post-Soviet system. An economic treaty was 
signed by eight republics at the end of October 1991, and the tri-partite agreement 
between Russia, Ukraine and Belarus, which formed the nucleus of the Commonwealth of 
Independent States, was settled in the first week of December.

HISTORY: 
SINCE THE BREAK-UP of the 
Soviet Union

The Russia Federation was the heartland of 
the former Soviet Union, with half its population. It is not a homogeneous entity, but 
hosts nearly 100 distinct nationalities and comprises 16 autonomous republics and 30 
autonomous areas. A number of these were the cause of major secessionist headaches for the 
Yeltsin government. 1991 and 1992 saw outbreaks of fighting in North Ossetia and 
Ingushetia, and tension is very high in the autonomous region of Bashkiria. Another worry 
has been the million-strong region of Tatarstan where an independence referendum in March 
1992 drew a 61% vote in favour. The most serious situation of all is in Chechnya, where 
full-scale civil war broke out in 1994 (see below). Yeltsin
â
s other main problem was 
the desperate condition of the Russian economy. He did not, however, deviate much from the 
path of reform, and after several poor years, the economy is now showing signs of 
recovery. This process is still at an early stage, however, and there is still widespread 
hardship and potential for unrest. The West has proved more sceptical and less forthcoming 
with financial aid than Yeltsin and his government had hoped. In the hope of unlocking a 
major potential source of aid, particularly for the eastern part of the country, the 
Yeltsin government has devoted some attention to improving relations with Japan. The issue 
which most concerns the Japanese is the future of the Kurile Islands which were occupied 
by the Red Army in 1945. The Japanese have offered the Russians US$2.5 billion in soft 
loans and technical assistance with the promise of up to US$15 billion, if sovereignty 
reverts to them. But Yeltsin is constrained, as Gorbachev was, by conservative resistance 
to territorial concessions. The principal opposition to Yeltsin was a coalition of 
conservative nationalists and communists which came together under the umbrella of a 
National Salvation Front, backed by powerful elements in the military, industry and 
elsewhere. Their ultimate aim was to replace Yeltsin with a coalition government. Their 
main powerbase was the Congress of People
â
s Deputies (CPD), the parliamentary body elected in 
the Gorbachev era. Relations between Yeltsin and the Congress, never good, deteriorated 
through 1992 as the Congress became the principal obstacle to Yeltsin
â
s economic 
reforms. Yeltsin appealed directly to the population for support for the continuation of 
the reform programme. A referendum in April 1993 won majority support, particularly in the 
cities, which was sufficient to confirm the Yeltsin policy programme. Prime Minister Yegor 
Gaidar lost the premiership (although he retained his more important advisory role) to an 
appointee of the CPD, Viktor Chernomyrdin. Despite this political victory, Yeltsin knew 
that the only real solution to the problem of congressional obstruction was to get a new 
Congress. He therefore announced, in September 1993, that new elections for the Congress 
would be held in December. This was, as Yeltsin himself later admitted, unconstitutional, 
and the Congress objected strongly. They argued that in issuing this decree, Yeltsin had 
exceeded his authority and if he failed to reverse it he would forfeit his position as 
President of the Russian Federation. This was the essential political conflict that 
produced the events in the first week of October 1993. A stand-off between the parties was 
followed by a siege of the Parliament building (the White House) and street fighting 
between the supporters of the Congress and Interior Ministry troops who remained loyal to 
Yeltsin. Inside the building, two former allies of Yeltsin, Alexander Rutskoi and Rutlan 
Khasbulatov, declared themselves, with the backing of the Congress, leaders of a 
provisional government in place of the supposedly illegal Yeltsin regime. The resolution 
of the conflict was eventually decided, not by constitutional niceties, but by the loyalty 
of the armed forces. Just as the security forces refused to fire on the Parliament 
building and backed Gorbachev and Yeltsin during the attempted coup in 1991, the army and 
Interior Ministry remained on Yeltsin
â
s side on this occasion. The White House was gutted 
and the leaders of the Congress, including Rutskoi and Khasbulatov, arrested. All other 
deputies were released after questioning.

A constitutional referendum and elections 
to a new bicameral parliament took place on December 12, 1993. The constitution draws 
heavily on the French and US models, emphasising the role of the president; the powers of 
the legislature are strictly limited. These were the first post-Soviet democratic 
elections in the Russian Federation. Although reformist groupings hold a majority in the 
Duma (Lower House), it was the showing of the ultra-nationalist, so-called Liberal 
Democrats, led by Vladimir Zhirinovsky, that caused consternation both inside and outside 
the Russian Federation. His party gained 64 of the 450 seats, to become the third largest 
party grouping. The reformist 
â
Russia
â
s Choice
â
 group gained 65 seats. Zhirinovsky
â
s success, 
despite his barely submerged racism and warmongering rhetoric, was attributed to public 
discontent with the hardship caused by economic reform and the decline of Russia
â
s 
international status. As far as Yeltsin was concerned, that the election was conducted 
fairly and without incident and the constitution accepted, constituted a success, although 
the results were hardly an endorsement of his policies. In the Federation Council, 57 
seats went to supporters of Yeltsin, 78 to centrists; opponents to the Government took 25 
seats. The most recent Duma elections, held in December 1995, saw Zhirinovsky
â
s share of 
the vote decline and his representation slip to 51 seats. The biggest winner on this 
occasion was the reconstituted Communist Party which 
â
 together with its allies in the Agrarian Party and 
smaller groupings from among the total of 42 parties which fought the election 
â
 commands 
189 seats. The party of the Prime Minister, Viktor Chernomyrdin, registered a 
disappointing 54 seats, while the reformers of Yabloko took 46. Other failures were Russia
â
s Choice 
with just 9 seats and the Congress of Russian Communities, led by popular ex-army general 
Alexander Lebed, with 5. A striking feature of the results was the division between the 
main metropolitan areas, which favoured reform-minded candidates, and the rest of the 
country, which leant strongly in favour of the Commmunists or Liberal Democrats. The 
election was widely seen as a dry run for the key presidential election to be held in June 
1996. Yeltsin is definitely standing for a second term, but the leading position in the 
polls is held by the Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov. After the initial alarm caused by 
the Communists
â
 performance in December 1995, Zyuganov has done his utmost to 
reassure a worried international community that a government under his control would not 
reverse wholesale the huge reforms that Russia
â
s society and economy have experienced since 1991. 
Other than maintaining the steady economic recovery, Zyuganov
â
s declared priorities are 
twofold: the settlement of regional conflicts, especially the bloody and costly civil war 
in Chechnya, and the restoration of Russia
â
s much damaged international prestige. Neither is 
easy. The Chechens have proved a tough and resourceful adversary and have tied down large 
numbers of Russian troops in a guerrilla campaign. Russian firepower is sufficient to 
prevent their defeat, but they have neither the military competence nor political 
direction to secure a victory and return the territory to Russian control. Several 
ceasefires and attempts at a peace agreement have failed. The second task of restoring the 
country
â
s international standing is equally daunting since Russia was shut out of the 
Middle East and cold-shouldered by the West in the Balkans. Relations with the West have 
been rather difficult since 1991, particularly as a result of what Moscow interprets as 
aggressive expansionism on the part of NATO, which is eager to recruit its former Warsaw 
Pact allies and even some of the former Soviet republics into its ranks. Russia is not 
being considered for NATO, as it has been offered membership of the more loosely conceived 
Partnership for Peace. Russia has joined the Council of Europe, however, and may achieve 
some form of associate membership of the European Union; but, as with NATO, full 
membership is not available. Concerns in the West about the dismissal in 1995 of Yeltsin
â
s 
pro-Western foreign minister Andrei Kozyrev have been eased by the appointment of 
ex-Washington Ambassador Yuri Vorontsov. 

GOVERNMENT: 
Under the new 
constitution introduced by referendum in 1993, a bicameral legislature and executive 
president are elected for 4-year terms. The State Duma (Lower House) consists of 450 
Deputies, half elected in single-member constituencies on a first-past-the-post basis and 
half according to party lists. The Federation Council consists of two representatives from 
each of the 89 constituent republics and regions, also elected on a first-past-the-post 
basis. The president nominates the prime minister who must then be endorsed by parliament. 
The president and the prime minister, together, appoint a government. 

Russian History from Bucknell University 
-- This site is considered by most to be the premier site on Russian 
    history on the WWW. It is interesting even for non-historians and regularly linked to by 
    universities, native Russians, and Russian travel companies. In addition to its articles, 
    it has an excellent 
chronology/timeline
 of Russian history as well as a superb diagrams of 
    the "
House of Rurik
" 
    and "
House of Romanov
."
 

Russia.NET
 
-- From SeaNet Corporation in Seattle, Washington, this site 
    presents a well-organized collection of articles on the history of Russia, beginning with 
    the origins of the Slavs in the 7
th
 Century BC. This sites strong suit is that 
    each article is clearly and concisely written. The last article on Russian history at this 
    site covers the failed coup of 1991 (in which Gorbachev stepped down); hence, Yeltsin's 
    presidency is not covered here.
 

Russian 
    National Tourist Office
 
-- Though this sites is 
    written for English-speaking tourists travelling to Russia. It offers a comprehensive, 
    summarized history of Russia that students and scholars would find interesting. This site 
    offers more detailed articles than most sites, but they are objective and easy to read. 

Treasures of the Czars

-- From the Florida International Museum and St. Petersburg 
    Times in Tampa, Florida, this site is the most state-of-the-art of all Russian history 
    sites. This site was developed for the opening of the Florida International Museum, whose 
    main attraction at the time was the rare collection of artifacts from the Czars. 
    Undoubtedly, this site provides the best review of the Czars and Russian leadership from 
    1613 to 1917, when the Bolsheviks seized power. In addition to an excellent 
timeline
 of the Czars, with 
    articles on each Czar, you can take a 
virtual tour
 of the museums 
    artifacts (owned by the Moscow Kremlin Museum) and see the prized possessions of Peter the 
    Great and other Czars. 

Index of 
    World History Links
 -- This is an exhaustive list 
    of hundreds of Internet resource links to virtually all eras and all civilizations in 
    world history. From the University of Kansas.

Other 
Top Links to Russian History

Timo 
    Hannukkala's Russian History Site
 -- From Tampere, 
    Finland, this site is new and presents several admirable in-depth articles on selected 
    aspects of Russian history. 

Russian History for 
    K-12 Teachers
 
-- From Dennis Boals and Xplore 
    Company, this site is designed to assist teachers in encouraging students to use the World 
    Wide Web as a tool for learning traditional subjects such as history. This site is 
    designed to be a "launch pad" to other research resources on the WWW. As such, 
    it has an extensive list of links on Russian history, but it doesn't have any articles. 

Brief Russian 
    History for Tourists
 
-- from Lonely Planet Travel Company. This is the highly condensed 
    version of Russian history. If you only have a minute, this would be the site to pick. 

Brief History of Russia
 -- from 
    University of Minnesota, the abridged Cliff Notes version of Russian history. 

Gateway to World History
 -- A huge 
    database that provides Internet resources in support of the study and teaching of world 
    history. 

Beyond 
    the Pale
 
-- History of Jews in Russia. The WWW 
    version of an exhibit that has recently toured in Russia, by Education Against Prejudice, 
    a non-profit organization. It is an in-depth, illustrated history of Jews in Russia, with 
    over 400 historical photographs.

Russian 
    Archives
 
-- The Library of Congress presents an 
    excellent repository of predominately 20
th
 century events and personalities, 
    such as Stalin's repression, attacks on the Intelligentsia, and Chernobyl.

    History Sources on the Internet
 -- From Betsy 
    Lauppe of the University of Washington (my alma mater). She has some links that are not

th

    History of Russia and the Former USSR
